thread.title: If You Want To Blame Someone For The U.S. Trade Deficit With China, Blame Apple - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: George Kesarios
title: If You Want To Blame Someone For The U.S. Trade Deficit With China, Blame Apple - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
When the U.S. administration first started threatening China with trade sanctions, I did not take it seriously. My first thoughts were that this is some kind of political stunt from the U.S. administration for local U.S. consumption. I never thought it would reach where we are today.
And to be sure, to date, what we are seeing is a simple skirmish. This is the reason why tariffs enacted thus far have not done any harm to markets. However, to the extent that both the U.S. and China do not settle their trade differences, markets will eventually be impacted.
To what extent is too early to tell, and hopefully, everyone will come to their senses. However, if no one blinks, initially the trade war will hurt the economy, but longer term a dollar shortage might emerge.
Who Is To Blame For The U.S. Trade Deficit With China? According to data from the BEA , the difference between goods imported to the U.S. from China and goods imported to China from the U.S. was $375B for 2017.
According to Apple's ( AAPL ) 2017 10-K report , revenue for the Americas was $96.6B. Apple does not break down U.S. revenue, so I will take a guess that U.S. revenue was $90B for 2017 (it might be less, but I am only trying to make a point).
In other words, of the $375B trade deficit the U.S. has with China, about $90B of that was generated by Apple alone. To put that in perspective, one company alone is responsible for about 24% of the trade deficit with China. My question is, does this actually count as a trade deficit?
Apple's supply chain is spread throughout the world, mainly in Asia. Even if we assume Apple produced everything in the U.S., the supply chain deficit would still exist.
But it gets even funnier. According to IHS Markit Inc. (via Bloomberg ), the iPhone X with 64 gigabytes of storage costs $370 to make, and the iPhone 8 (base model) around $255. The average selling price for iPhone X is $999 and $699 for the iPhone 8. So, excluding marketing and R&D costs, Apple makes about $629 from the iPhone X, and $444 from every iPhone 8 sold.
But guess what, this money comes back to the U.S. in Apple's bank account. Apple's money was never overseas, but in foreign bank branches located in the U.S. So in reality, the trade deficit Apple is responsible for with China is a lot less. In fact, probably 50% less.
I can probably name at least another 100 U.S. companies that either outsource or have a manufacturing base in China and import goods to the U.S. And if we calculate the profits that come from overseas, minus the cost to make these imported goods to the U.S. (from U.S. companies as I said), the U.S. might actually have a surplus with China, not a deficit. So, if President Trump wants to point fingers, he better start with Apple and then follow up with all the other companies in the S&P 500 Index ( SPY ).
As was reported recently, Harley-Davidson ( HOG ) announced it will move some of its production outside of the US in response to the 31% trade tariffs announced by the EU (European Union).
The company said that the average price of its motorcycles shipped from the U.S. to Europe will increase by $2,200. The company also said that it will absorb the $90 million to $100 million per yearly cost.
In a regulatory filing , the company said:
Harley-Davidson believes the tremendous cost increase, if passed onto its dealers and retail customers, would have an immediate and lasting detrimental impact to its business in the region , reducing customer access to Harley-Davidson products and negatively impacting the sustainability of its dealers' businesses. Therefore, Harley-Davidson will not raise its manufacturer's suggested retail prices or wholesale prices to its dealers to cover the costs of the retaliatory tariffs. In the near-term, the company will bear the significant impact resulting from these tariffs, and the company estimates the incremental cost for the remainder of 2018 to be approximately $30 to $45 million. On a full-year basis, the company estimates the aggregate annual impact due to the EU tariffs to be approximately $90 to $100 million.
To address the substantial cost of this tariff burden long-term, Harley-Davidson will be implementing a plan to shift production of motorcycles for EU destinations from the U.S. to its international facilities to avoid the tariff burden. Harley-Davidson expects ramping- up production in international plants will require incremental investment and could take at least 9 to 18 months to be fully complete.
So, on the one hand, jobs will be moved overseas and second, the trade deficit will widen because Harley-Davidson will now manufacture bikes in Europe. That not being enough, the policy will also destroy shareholder value. In other words, the President's policy has totally backfired.
Populism For Local Consumption It's really sad to see politicians and economists advocating the policies the U.S. administration is pushing for. The main reason is because they will have the opposite effect of what president Trump is trying to accomplish.
The U.S. is neither losing jobs as result of the trade deficit nor is getting poorer. If that were the case, it would have been poor already, with sky-high unemployment. But as you know this is not the case.
The problem with all these policies is not that the U.S. will not win, it will. The problem is that in the end, it will lose as a result of a rising dollar.
As I wrote a short while ago, by default, a stronger U.S. dollar is bad for markets (please consider: A Stronger Dollar Is Negative For Markets Around The World ). The problem with a stronger dollar is that it causes stress in the emerging markets space and tightens financial conditions for everyone.
The reason has to do with the $11.4 trillion in dollar-denominated debt that is outside the jurisdiction of the Fed. So, on the one hand when the dollar rises those who have borrowed in dollars have to pay more in local currency, and on the other, several hundred billion in interest has to be paid on this debt.
This is what happens when such conditions last for long periods:
A dollar shortage problem emerges This, in turn, creates "tightened financial conditions" Investors stop undertaking risk Initially, emerging markets tumble and mature markets follow Massive wealth is lost Consumer confidence declines The economy is impacted Recession fears emerge Central banks to the rescue Believe it or not, all of the above might happen if President Trump insists on lowering the trade deficit with China and several other countries. Because by lowering the trade deficit, eventually a dollar demand might emerge.
And because dollars can only trickle down to the rest of world by means of a U.S. trade and current account deficit, it is very important the U.S. continues to have a trade deficit. You are not reading a typo, the U.S. and the world need a U.S trade deficit.
Bottom Line If President Trump wants to point fingers, Apple and most companies listed on the S&P 500 Index is a great place to start, instead of blaming China or any other country.
While there is a lot of talk in the financial press about the impact of a trade war on the economy, there is very little talk about a bigger problem, that of a dollar shortage if the U.S. trade deficit shrinks.
So, keep an eye on the dollar. If you see a sudden rise, it might mean there is a shortage of dollars worldwide, that might impact markets very hard.
